title: Political fallout from Trump’s Russian diesel deal overshadows price impact
author: Eleanor Mueller
text: From Semafor Washington, DCIn your inbox, every weekdaySign upPolitical fallout from Trump’s Russian diesel deal overshadows price impactUpdated Oct 14, 2026, 9:44am UTCPostEmailWhatsappSputnik/Gavriil Grigorov/Pool via Reuters President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin’s deal to deliver Russian diesel to global markets may be sending shockwaves through the GOP — but don’t expect it to do the same to prices. Already, multiple House Republicans; key GOP candidates; and two bipartisan groups of senators have pushed back on the move. The planned imports will “have very little unnoticeable impact on domestic US diesel prices, even if it happens — and I think that’s a big if,” given legal complications and Russian constraints, Bloomberg economist Chris Kennedy, who served on the National Security Council during the Trump and Biden administrations, told Semafor. He said that the amount of diesel Russia has pledged to release for the month of November represents only “one day of US diesel demand.”He pointed to heating oil futures, observing that “traders appear to be pricing in very little near-term impact.” The White House pushed back: One official insisted to Semafor that “massive amounts of supply will lower costs for American farmers, truckers and workers.”“They’re not releasing that [diesel] to us, they’re releasing it to the entire world,” Trump told reporters Tuesday. “Because the world market suffered with high prices — and when you knock out diesel refineries, that’s not a great thing.” — Eleanor MuellerMore from Semafor Washington, DCFAA equity talks raise questions about the agency’s legal authorityTariffs pose a risk to US-India relationship Zacharia’s rocky stint as press secretary endsUS-Ukraine rift not affecting weapons Trump administration logs record foreign investmentConservative AI safety group proposes export controls, visa restrictionsFAA equity talks raise questions about the agency’s legal authorityUpdated Oct 16, 2026, 8:14pm UTCPostEmailWhatsappLindsey Wasson/ReutersThe Federal Aviation Administration’s pursuit of an equity stake in a private company that uses AI to manage air traffic is raising questions about whether it has clear legal authority to strike such a deal.The Trump administration has negotiated stakes in dozens of other companies, but none through the FAA. The agency’s interest in owning part of Air Space Intelligence, first reported by Politico, is too “premature” for there to be specifics, a person familiar with the matter told Semafor. Talks so far have been limited to a handful of internal conversations, the person added. One possible statutory underpinning for a deal: Existing law authorizes Transportation Department financial help for state or local governments to “acquire an interest” in some public transportation companies. That argument, like other agencies’, would be a stretch. “It’s further proof that the administration doesn’t have a ‘plan’ or ‘strategy,’” said Tad DeHaven, who tracks the stakes for the Cato Institute.— Eleanor Mueller and Shelby TalcottADTariffs pose a risk to US-India relationship Updated Oct 16, 2026, 8:08pm UTCPostEmailWhatsappNathan Howard/ReutersPresident Donald Trump faces a deadline Sunday to decide whether to impose certain penalties on other countries under a bipartisan sanctions law he signed last month.Any move by him to waive sanctions on Russian individuals or entities will be met with criticism, as would a decision not to impose tariffs on China for buying Russian gas. But Washington is hoping he’ll spare at least one country: India. “Both the United States and India should not buy Russian oil and gas, but I don’t think simply imposing big tariffs on India is the way to get them to” reduce their purchases, said Richard Fontaine, CEO of the Center for a New American Security. Punishing India for its reliance on Russian energy “would deal a body blow to the US-India relationship,” argued Sadanand Dhume, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.The US and India are currently locked in trade negotiations, which more tariffs would surely disrupt. Fontaine said it is “100%” possible that the Trump administration uses the sanctions law to pressure India to give in to its demands in those discussions. Trump had previously hiked tariffs on India over its Russian energy purchases, but later removed them as trade talks progressed.Asked whether Trump had made a decision on which sanctions, if any, to impose at the deadline, a White House official said that he “signed the act and the administration will comply with the act’s requirements.” The bill gives the president broad power to waive penalties if he deems it in the US interest.— Morgan ChalfantZacharia’s rocky stint as press secretary endsUpdated Oct 16, 2026, 8:01pm UTCPostEmailWhatsappKylie Cooper/ReutersKatie Zacharia is out as White House press secretary after less than one week on the job. An administration official told Semafor that Zacharia will be “transitioning out” of her role, which began on Monday and quickly descended into a series of stumbles, culminating in Fox News pressing her earlier today on whether she regretted not being clearer about her failure to pass the bar exam. Moments before news broke of her departure from the role, President Donald Trump said he told Zacharia “you don’t have to do this,” but suggested he’d give her the decision to stay or leave. One source familiar with the situation emphasized to Semafor that Trump remains a fan of hers, adding that Zacharia and her family are planning to dine with Vice President JD Vance and his family at his residence tonight.— Shelby TalcottADUS-Ukraine rift not affecting weapons Updated Oct 16, 2026, 8:57am UTCPostEmailWhatsappValentyn Ogirenko/Reuters The US’ relationship with Ukraine has reached a new low — but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s current spat with Trump hasn’t affected the flow of US weapons to his country. The Pentagon has communicated to NATO members that a US procurement program that sends weapons to Ukraine via NATO is continuing uninterrupted, a European official told Semafor, echoing comments made by the US ambassador to NATO earlier this week.That doesn’t mean that European officials aren’t worried about the prospect of a lapse in weapons, as CNN reported; Trump has reportedly considered suspending arms shipments along with intelligence-sharing, and the Starlink slowdown Ukrainians suffered earlier this week was the result of an order from the White House, Reuters reported. Zelenskyy’s decision to resume strikes on Russian refineries may further strain ties. US lawmakers, however, are still demonstrating bipartisan support for Ukraine’s fight. — Morgan ChalfantExclusive / Trump administration logs record foreign investmentEleanor MuellerWhite House Reporter, SemaforUpdated Oct 16, 2026, 8:56am UTCPostEmailWhatsappJonathan Ernst/Reuters The Commerce Department’s SelectUSA program has secured more foreign direct investment under President Donald Trump than its previous dozen-plus years combined, officials told Semafor. That’s $280 billion from firms like Singapore’s Bitdeer, Australia’s Graphinex, Belgium’s UCB, South Korea’s Korea Zinc, and Japan’s Isuzu Motors, spread across more than 345 projects. The program, launched in 2011, had previously brought in a total of $255 billion. Assistant Commerce Secretary David Fogel attributed the bump to the Trump administration’s efforts to scrap regulations and lower taxes — and its blunt use of tariffs, which have at times strained its relationships with trading partners. “One of the elements of that [agenda] is using tariffs as a leverage tool to exact investment commitments from foreign countries,” Fogel told Semafor. With the midterms less than three weeks away, Fogel argued that’s a “promise [to voters] kept,” since Trump “definitely ran on a pro-worker agenda, and now we’re seeing the follow-through on that in terms of hitting these record numbers.” ADExclusive / Conservative AI safety group proposes export controls, visa restrictionsAshley GoldSenior Tech CorrespondentUpdated Oct 16, 2026, 8:56am UTCPostEmailWhatsappManuel Orbegozo/Reuters Humans First, a conservative-led group advocating for stronger AI guardrails, is out with an “America First AI Policy” platform on Friday, according to a memo shared first with Semafor. Key parts of the framework include tightening export controls against China and other adversaries; mandating independent testing for large AI companies; prohibiting the development of advanced AI practices like recursive self-improvement; banning federal use of cameras like Flock; requiring public reporting of AI incidents; and ensuring that frontier AI developers can be held liable for reckless conduct. The group also wants strict rules for AI used by children and calls for a pause on H-1B visas. “An AI policy that truly puts America First is centered around the American people — not globalist corporations and not unaccountable bureaucrats,” said Russ Walker, the group’s executive director and an adviser to President Donald Trump’s 2020 campaign. “It is time for Congress to act and it is time for conservatives in particular to lead on this critical issue.”The group is chaired by Amy Kremer, a longtime Tea Party activist who argues Republicans are missing an opportunity to lead on AI policy that doesn’t cater to big companies. She’s been leading a bus tour across the country dubbed the “AI Data Center Revolt.” The framework’s priorities go beyond what some Republicans who are interested in regulating AI on Capitol Hill have proposed, and significantly further than the Trump administration’s current light touch on AI. Still, this vocal group may have more sway going forward if Republicans perform poorly in the midterms and AI anxiety is a factor.Top StoriesWhy Suntory’s CEO is still investing in a sobered-up spirits marketZacharia’s rocky stint as press secretary endsKylie Cooper/ReutersThe UAE’s ‘Zero Hormuz’ strategy runs through Fujairah Kevin Zweerink/SemaforAOC and El-Sayed test-drive a national platform for the leftNicholas Wu/SemaforThe $22B startup co-founder working to make chatbots talk back US-Ukraine rift not affecting weapons Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters Trump administration logs record foreign investmentJonathan Ernst/Reuters Lowball retention bonuses doomed Perella-Piper Sandler mergerDado Ruvic/Illustration/ReutersThe Worldat a GlanceUS stocks recover after multi-day tech selloffUpdated Oct 15, 2026, 10:23pm UTCPostEmailWhatsappJeenah Moon/ReutersUS stocks clawed back losses Thursday following a multi-day tech selloff, as investors flocked to safer assets on concerns the AI buildout could falter in the face of weak consumer demand and high inflation. US producer prices increased at the fastest pace in four years in September, new data showed, bolstering the case for the Federal Reserve to hike rates this month. Bumper earnings from AI-exposed firms this week have failed to quell fears that higher rates could halt or slow the debt-fueled data center buildout that’s currently powering the US economy. Still, some of the AI trade’s biggest spenders appear undeterred: TSMC said Thursday it was building plants at an “unprecedented pace” and could expand its US footprint further on “extremely robust” AI demand.— Brendan RuberryAI infrastructure debt costs soar amid investor concernsUpdated Oct 16, 2026, 11:08am UTCPostEmailWhatsappCoreWeave CEO and founder Michael Intrator. Brendan McDermid/ReutersYields on a key cloud provider’s bonds rose further, one of a number of signs of investors souring on AI infrastructure investment. The cost to insure CoreWeave’s bonds has also risen 150% from a year ago, while its stock at one point fell 28% this week. It is not the only firm investors are worried about, either: Oracle’s $160 billion debt is rated just above junk status, and Microsoft’s AAA-rated debt costs 25% more to insure than three months ago. Ultimately, AI “is probably the most consequential change to the … economy in my lifetime,” Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh said. But “the path from where we are to there is likely to be a bumpy one.”— Prashant RaoApple and Meta to collaborate on new AI modelUpdated Oct 16, 2026, 11:29am UTCPostEmailWhatsappCarlos Barria/ReutersApple and Meta said they would join forces to release a new open-weight AI model to run on high-end Macs, the latest sign of AI reshaping old tech rivalries and building new ones. The giants have been at odds for more than a decade: Meta has complained that Apple’s app store policies have cost it billions, while the Facebook owner’s CEO reportedly told his team to “inflict pain” on the iPhone maker. By teaming up, they aim to offer a US open-weight model to compete both with rival Chinese offerings and the closed systems built by frontier labs Anthropic and OpenAI. “We’re excited for mommy and daddy to be playing nice again,” Meta’s AI chief Alexandr Wang told Axios.— Prashant RaoTaipei restricts China chip sales to appease the USUpdated Oct 16, 2026, 11:07am UTCPostEmailWhatsappFlorence Lo/ReutersTaiwan is set to tighten controls on selling cutting-edge AI chips to China in order to win favor with the US, though breakthroughs by Chinese firms suggest Washington’s efforts to contain their development are failing. The latest move by Taipei — a central node in global semiconductor manufacturing — is a significant step in curtailing black market sales to Chinese companies seeking to bypass US curbs. China’s own firms appear to be making headway in building up their own capacity, however: Though US companies are still seen as leading on chip design, Chinese ones are increasingly taking domestic AI-chip market share from US giant Nvidia, Reuters reported, with Huawei in particular passing key milestones in recent days.— Prashant RaoTrade talks between the US, Mexico in jeopardyUpdated Oct 16, 2026, 11:08am UTCPostEmailWhatsappJose Luis Gonzalez/ReutersThe US appeared to step back from progress on a trade deal with Mexico. US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s reported insistence that steel, aluminum, and car levies remain in place with Washington’s biggest commercial partner has thrown the negotiations into question. An expert warned that further undoing the countries’ trilateral free trade agreement with Canada could “jeopardize the financial health” of many American companies, while making US goods more expensive. Elsewhere, however, trade talks between Washington and New Delhi appeared to be gaining momentum — despite US President Donald Trump imposing 100% tariffs on buyers of Russian oil, of which India is the world’s second-biggest. “The big picture, the big framework, the big items are done,” Washington’s ambassador to India said.— Jeronimo GonzalezTesla and Porsche unveil new models as competition with China heats upUpdated Oct 16, 2026, 11:10am UTCPostEmailWhatsappTesla’s Roadster using its cold-gas thrusters. Tesla/Handout via ReutersTwo major Western car makers announced new flagship vehicles as they vie to keep up with Chinese challengers. Tesla unveiled its Roadster, first touted almost a decade ago, while Porsche revealed its first car under its new boss, who has vowed to turn the automaker’s fortunes around after years of declining sales, notably in China. However, the new models are not expected for years, contrasting with Chinese carmakers that have “slashed” production times, going from concept to launch in roughly 24 months, McKinsey said. Soaring output in China has pushed Europe and the US to throw up trade barriers, though those could prove ineffective. “Chinese cars on US roads is a matter of when, not if,” a Reuters columnist argued.— Jeronimo GonzalezZelenskyy meets EU leaders as his rift with Trump deepensUpdated Oct 15, 2026, 10:26pm UTCPostEmailWhatsappAlina Smutko/ReutersEU leaders are expected to ask Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy to moderate his rhetoric against US President Donald Trump amid Kyiv’s widening rift with Washington, the Financial Times reported. Zelenskyy and Trump have engaged in a war of words this week, with the former defying Washington’s directive to stop striking Russian refineries and accusing Trump of “loving” autocrats: “It might be true,” a European official said. “But it doesn’t always need to be said out loud.” The EU is concerned such diatribes could further destabilize the fragile transatlantic relationship. Still, past reconciliations with Washington have proven largely futile for Kyiv, a former US diplomat argued: Zelenskyy “flattered and thanked Trump, agreed to all his crazy ideas... and still got screwed.”— Brendan RuberryAirports are becoming targets in escalating warsUpdated Oct 15, 2026, 10:28pm UTCPostEmailWhatsappStringer/ReutersCivilian airports are increasingly becoming military targets, as nations at war seek new ways to inflict economic and psychological damage. Ukraine, under US pressure to stop striking Russian refineries, has expanded its targets — bombing data centers and clogging air space — while considering more aggressive tactics like directly hitting Russian airports, The Atlantic reported. Kyiv said Thursday it only responds in kind “to specific Russian strikes.” Such a shift would intensify threats to global aviation safety: The Houthis have reportedly struck Riyadh’s airport 20 times this month, clouding Saudi Arabia’s investment outlook; Germany accused Russia of attempting to bomb Leipzig’s airport in August; and an Iran-linked threat prompted the US to remove bombers from a UK airfield earlier this month.— Brendan RuberryUK signals it could coordinate with EU on Chinese EV tariffs Updated Oct 15, 2026, 10:34pm UTCPostEmailWhatsappStephanie Lecocq/ReutersThe UK said Thursday it was prepared to align its tariffs on Chinese EVs with those of the EU, delivering a boost to Brussels as it negotiates with Beijing to narrow the trade gap. European leaders have adopted a more aggressive stance to shield native businesses from a tidal wave of Chinese imports, which policymakers have blamed for deep job losses among European automakers and other sectors. So far, counter-efforts have involved both protectionist and industrial policies, including “Made in Europe” rules that have stoked discord among some of Europe’s largest economies. Having won Beijing’s agreement to halve hybrid vehicle imports, Brussels is now eyeing checks on Chinese chemicals and machinery, Politico reported.— Brendan RuberryUS expands military campaign against drug cartels in Latin AmericaUpdated Oct 15, 2026, 10:31pm UTCPostEmailWhatsappJose Cabezas/ReutersThe US is sending hundreds of soldiers to Latin America as the Pentagon widens its campaign against drug traffickers, The New York Times reported. A 600-strong battalion is reportedly being deployed to Panama; the head of a research group that tracks such deployments said he could not recall one “that ever came close to 600 except for contingencies like invasions or natural disasters.” President Donald Trump has made fighting cartels a priority of his second term, but US strikes on alleged drug traffickers have done little to dent the global cocaine trade, with shipments rising to record levels. Washington’s policy “is more about visibility and narrative… than one that genuinely disrupts organized crime,” an expert told The Wall Street Journal.— Tasneem NashrullaTrump cancels plans for execution livestream after blowbackUpdated Oct 15, 2026, 10:28pm UTCPostEmailWhatsappJonathan Ernst/ReutersUS President Donald Trump canceled his defense secretary’s plan to livestream the execution of a former military officer after widespread backlash. More than 70 retired military leaders condemned the “barbaric” order. The last known US public execution was in 1936, and only Iran and Afghanistan still regularly perform them. The New Yorker’s Dexter Filkins recalled watching a Taliban-staged execution in Kabul, writing: “What I saw was different, but not by much.” Hegseth suggested a public death would deter similar actions, but a historian argued that “Americans at the republic’s founding debated that premise.” A former military officer who studied execution videos wrote, “no sane person enjoys looking at an execution… to do so for the crass purpose of entertainment is even worse.”— Brendan RuberryTraders sour on AI stocks despite bumper third-quarter revenuesUpdated Oct 15, 2026, 10:55am UTCPostEmailWhatsappKim Hong-Ji/ReutersBumper earnings from bellwether tech giants Anthropic and TSMC did little to assuage a market that has turned bearish on the AI trade, sending stocks plummeting. The frontier AI lab said its third-quarter revenue grew more than threefold compared to the first three months of the year, while the Taiwanese chipmaker reported a sixth consecutive record quarterly profit. Yet as one analyst put it, at least in the case of Anthropic, traders were “increasingly concerned about the side effects of sustaining that growth”: Namely, the huge infrastructure buildout and the massive debt issuance funding it, with one AI cloud computing provider seeing yields on its bonds touching 15%. S&P futures — like Asian stocks — were down.— Prashant RaoSmartphone sales drop as chip costs soarUpdated Oct 15, 2026, 10:58am UTCPostEmailWhatsappTingshu Wang/ReutersGlobal smartphone shipments during the third quarter fell to their lowest level in 14 years, as a memory chip supply crunch pressured manufacturers to raise prices. As a result, consumers are keeping their devices for longer, and many have turned to refurbishments, an analyst at research firm Counterpoint said. Soft demand has hit Apple, the world’s second-biggest supplier after Samsung, particularly hard — October data showed the US tech giant, which relies on phone sales for around 50% of its revenue, reduced orders for the iPhone 18 by 15-20%. But it’s not just Apple in trouble: Transsion, a Chinese maker of low-cost phones sold mostly in Africa, is also under pressure, with its shares falling 7% in their Hong Kong debut.— Jeronimo GonzalezThreats to global shipping grow, amid a rise in attacksUpdated Oct 15, 2026, 11:00am UTCPostEmailWhatsappA recent spate of attacks on ships has piled further pressure on maritime traffic, which is already grappling with an array of challenges that are hampering trade and transport. Two cargo ships sunk near the Strait of Hormuz were the latest victims of an apparent surge in Iranian attacks, while Yemen’s Houthis have sought to strangle flows through the Red Sea. Nearby, piracy off the Horn of Africa coast has increased to its highest level since 2013, according to AFP analysis; further afield, suspected Russian drones hit two commercial ships near Bulgaria’s territorial waters. Conflict and unrest are not the only threats: Panama Canal traffic is currently congested because of drier conditions resulting from the El Niño weather pattern.— Prashant RaoChina and North Korea open new bridge as ties improveUpdated Oct 15, 2026, 11:10am UTCPostEmailWhatsappFlorence Lo/ReutersChina and North Korea opened their biggest land crossing, a sign of closer bilateral ties that are likely to unsettle regional countries. The 3 km (1.9 mile) Yalu River Bridge was first proposed more than 12 years ago, though it was delayed after ties between Beijing and Pyongyang turned frosty. Relations have improved in recent years thanks in large part to China’s strategic competition with the US, and as Beijing looks to manage Pyongyang’s growing ties to Moscow. The reset in relations has led China to ease demands on North Korea to denuclearize, raising fears across the region. “The implications for the United States and its allies are stark,” the Sydney-based Lowy Institute wrote.— Jeronimo GonzalezUkraine to restart strikes on Russian refineriesUpdated Oct 15, 2026, 10:59am UTCPostEmailWhatsappThe aftermath of a Russian strike on Kyiv. Anna Voitenko/Reuters.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy pledged to restart strikes against Russian oil refineries in anger over what he said was the US withdrawal of intelligence support for Kyiv. Washington has pressed Zelenskyy to curb attacks on energy facilities, linking them to the rising price of US fuel in the run-up to midterm elections, where Republicans are expected to fare poorly. The dispute between the countries has now erupted into a public row: US President Donald Trump called for Zelenskyy to be ousted, while the Ukrainian president, in an interview with the Financial Times, voiced frustration with his American counterpart’s warmth towards autocrats and blamed the White House for the deterioration in ties: “We didn’t destroy any relationship,” Zelenskyy told the FT.— Prashant RaoKenya hikes fuel prices to tame government costsUpdated Oct 15, 2026, 11:05am UTCPostEmailWhatsappMonicah Mwangi/ReutersKenya hiked fuel prices in order to contain surging government spending sparked by the war in the Middle East, which has badly exposed Africa’s reliance on energy imports. The increases put state-mandated prices of petrol and diesel 20% and 31% above prewar levels, respectively, pushing inflation in September to the highest rate in almost three years. Countries across Africa are reeling from higher fuel costs, sparking unrest and grinding economies to a standstill: Motorists in Malawi are sleeping at gas stations, sometimes for days, in the hopes of being there when supplies arrive. Record prices in South Africa, meanwhile, have pushed households to turn to firewood, coal, illegal electrical connections, “and other dangerous alternatives,” The Sowetan reported.— Jeronimo GonzalezUkraine’s leader says US is not on ‘right side of history’Updated Oct 14, 2026, 10:28pm UTCPostEmailWhatsappHenry Nicholls/Pool via ReutersUkraine’s leader said he felt betrayed by US President Donald Trump, blaming Washington and Elon Musk’s SpaceX for cutting off Kyiv’s Starlink use on Wednesday. “This is not the right side of history,” Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Piers Morgan, as relations between the two countries deteriorated. Kyiv and its allies fear that Washington is applying pressure tactics, including potentially cutting off intelligence sharing and restricting Starlink, “to force Ukraine to capitulate to Russia,” the Financial Times’ Ukraine correspondent wrote. Kyiv later said SpaceX had restored access, while Musk asserted any limits on access are decided by Trump. Ukrainian officials complained the earlier disruptions had hampered military capabilities as Russia rained down missiles, plunging 600,000 into darkness overnight. “People will die,” Zelenskyy said. — Brendan RuberryIran ramps up ship strikes in Hormuz ahead of US midterms Updated Oct 14, 2026, 10:30pm UTCPostEmailWhatsappStringer/ReutersIran’s increasing attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz have made October one of the most violent months in the waterway since the war began, as Tehran looks to exploit US President Donald Trump’s political vulnerability ahead of midterm elections. Two Emirati cargo vessels sank in the past 24 hours after being struck; Iranian officials told Reuters that Tehran was deliberately ramping up strikes to keep oil prices elevated before Nov. 3. Washington’s lack of response is “remarkable,” a Eurasia Group analyst said: “Trump continues to promise action, but only after [midterms].” That’s also when Washington could be more amenable to joining Saudi Arabia’s strikes against the Houthis, another analyst suggested: “Trump’s preference is for it to happen afterwards.”— Brendan RuberryInflation report raises Fed rate-hike oddsUpdated Oct 14, 2026, 8:12pm UTCPostEmailWhatsappEvan Vucci/ReutersInvestors are bracing for the Federal Reserve to again hike interest rates after the Labor Department said Wednesday that consumer prices rose more in September than economists had expected. The inflation report, which comes two weeks before the central bank’s next meeting and three weeks before Election Day, is heightening concerns about the Iran war’s effect on the cost of goods beyond food and energy. With consumer sentiment already nearing a record low, the Trump administration is frantically trying to put a positive spin on the data — and discourage the central bank from acting. Adviser Kevin Hassett told Fox Business it’s a “blip,” while adviser Peter Navarro wrote an editorial on why it proves “the Fed should hold its fire.” All eyes are on Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who is slated to speak in Bangkok later this week. — Eleanor MuellerOpenAI employee arrested over office buggingUpdated Oct 14, 2026, 10:26pm UTCPostEmailWhatsappDepartment of Justice/Handout via ReutersThe FBI on Tuesday said it arrested an OpenAI employee who was fired after allegedly bugging the startup’s office. The evidence against Abdulrahman Alfozan — a Saudi national who holds ties to Riyadh’s business elite — included chatbot logs about how to install recording devices, authorities said, rekindling fears over AI-powered crimes at a moment of heightened sensitivity over tech trade secrets. “The FBI’s quick work and public rollout of the arrest shows how high the stakes are for the US government and frontier labs,” Semafor’s Rohan Goswami wrote. The FBI’s announcement comes as the White House’s AI task force prepares for its first meeting Thursday; the group’s chair said the case proved why “the Super Intelligence Force is so important.”— Brendan RuberryUS Treasury says big banks discriminated on political groundsUpdated Oct 14, 2026, 10:28pm UTCPostEmailWhatsappAndrew Kelly/ReutersThe US Treasury’s “debanking” probe found that the largest American banks had denied services to customers based on political considerations, in a boost to conservatives’ campaign against institutions’ perceived biases. US President Donald Trump ordered the inquiry last year after he accused banks of discriminating against him, and sued JPMorgan Chase and Capital One for closing his accounts. The report comes one day after the government fined Bank of America $1.2 billion for lax money-laundering oversight, the third-largest penalty in Treasury history. The Trump administration has similarly targeted universities and media companies: The White House played a central role in the Justice Department’s antitrust investigation into major TV networks’ temporary suspension of pooled coverage of the president, Semafor reported Wednesday.— Brendan RuberryApple gears up for AI product push in ChinaUpdated Oct 14, 2026, 10:32pm UTCPostEmailWhatsappTingshu Wang/ReutersApple’s first foldable smartphone will feature Alibaba’s AI when it launches in China next week, as Apple Intelligence — the company’s generative suite — gears up for its mainland appearance after years of regulatory delays. Apple sees AI features as critical to competing with Huawei, the only firm it lags in China. The world’s largest smartphone market has slumped amid weak consumer spending and rising hardware costs. Still, China’s cutthroat industry is seeing new entrants: AI lab StepFun launched a $600 AI agent smartphone Tuesday. An analyst described the move as “quite bold” under present conditions, but one that might be explained by the smartphone’s unparalleled ability to continually gather user data, allowing AI assistants to become ever-more personalized.— Brendan RuberryChinese exports surge, putting the country on track for a record surplusUpdated Oct 14, 2026, 11:28am UTCPostEmailWhatsappChina Daily/ReutersChinese exports jumped 36% year-on-year in September, a bumper figure that is likely to vex the country’s trade partners, who have demanded Beijing address imbalances and alleged domestic overproduction. Faced with US and EU restrictions, which have dented Chinese imports in the West, Chinese companies have turned to other markets, sparking criticism from producers in Southeast Asia and Africa, who say their industries risk being hollowed out. The latest figures pushed China’s trade surplus in 2026 to almost $1 trillion, nearing the entire figure for last year, underlining the country’s continued reliance on exports, with domestic consumption weighed down by a long-running real estate crash and rising youth unemployment. Beijing has so far resisted calls for a significant stimulus package.— Jeronimo GonzalezASML CEO confident AI demand will outstrip supply for years to comeUpdated Oct 14, 2026, 11:29am UTCPostEmailWhatsappYves Herman/ReutersThe CEO of ASML, the world’s only provider of the machines that make cutting-edge chips, said AI demand would outstrip supply for years to come, easing investors’ worries of a spending bubble. His comments come after Europe’s most valuable company reported bumper profits that far exceeded analyst expectations, boosting its share price. Investors globally have grown concerned that AI spending may be cresting as borrowing costs surge, with the International Monetary Fund warning that a market correction posed a threat to the global economy. But, for now, spending on the technology remains strong: Goldman Sachs expects AI infrastructure investment to drive a $7.6 trillion boom through 2031.— Jeronimo GonzalezCopper prices near record highs over threat of Chile mine strikeUpdated Oct 14, 2026, 11:30am UTCPostEmailWhatsappIvan Alvarado/ReutersThe threat of a worker’s strike — which has since been averted — at Chile’s La Escondida, the world’s biggest copper mine, sent prices for the metal near record levels, underscoring the Latin American country’s growing role in the industry. Other recent temporary closures in some of Chile’s copper mines, which are responsible for almost a quarter of global output, because of worker accidents and benefits disputes have also pushed up international prices. Demand for the metal has surged on the back of the AI data center and EV production boom, with countries globally racing to lock up supplies. But despite production rising to record levels in 2025, UBS nonetheless expects shortfalls to reach an all-time high next year.— Jeronimo GonzalezHouthis reportedly strike Saudi national oil company headquartersUpdated Oct 14, 2026, 11:31am UTCPostEmailWhatsappAn attack on the Riyadh airport. Saudi Ministry of Media/Handout via ReutersIran-backed Houthi fighters reportedly hit the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s national oil company in overnight strikes, stoking a conflict that risks spiralling into a wider war. The attacks follow a Houthi onslaught that killed 13, injured hundreds, and forced Riyadh’s airport to shut at least through Saturday, denting the kingdom’s reputation for stability and piling pressure on the country’s de facto ruler. Analysts fear the conflict could expand beyond the Arabian Peninsula: The Houthis are reportedly building an advanced missile using Chinese parts. US President Donald Trump has accused the group of “purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices” ahead of November’s midterm elections; Tehran is reportedly targeting crude tankers in a bid to keep prices elevated.— Jeronimo GonzalezIndia cracks down on growing protestsUpdated Oct 14, 2026, 11:32am UTCPostEmailWhatsappPriyanshu Singh/ReutersIndia cracked down further on anti-government protests that have grown substantially in recent months, escalating from attacking the authorities over education to frustration with what critics see as broader threats to the country’s democracy. Three leaders of an upstart political party were jailed and an historic protest site in central New Delhi — “the country’s most recognizable stage for public dissent,” per AFP — was shut down. The latest demonstrations have centered around a review of India’s electoral rolls that has led to an estimated 130 million people being barred from voting. Opponents of the effort say it has targeted minorities and critics of the ruling Hindu nationalist party; in Delhi, for example, The Hindu reported that Muslims were disproportionately affected.— Prashant RaoSpain’s king says control of country’s African territories is ‘non-negotiable’Updated Oct 14, 2026, 11:33am UTCPostEmailWhatsappPedro Nunes/ReutersSpain’s king said his country’s control of exclaves in Africa was “non-negotiable,” after the cities became flashpoints in territorial disputes with Morocco and Europe’s anti-immigration debate.
